title: Neuromuscular Coordination and Balance
summary:
Pregnancy brings a forward-shifting center of gravity, increased uterine volume and weight, ligamentous laxity and gait changes, all of which impair balance and coordination. Training these qualities helps maintain postural control, respond to disturbances, move safely and reduce falls, which matter for both mother and fetus. It also helps women adapt movement patterns, do other exercises with better technique, and feel more confident and consistent.

The chapter describes static and dynamic balance, functional coordination, stabilization, reaction and aquatic exercises, each with pregnancy adaptations. Programming varies by fitness level, with trimester adjustments and a sample micro-session. Specific evidence in pregnancy is limited, but existing studies and guidelines support including a neuromotor component with supervision and no medical contraindications.
points: Single-leg stance is held 10-30 s and tandem stance 20-30 s, starting at 10 s and increasing to 20 s as tolerated.
Step-downs use a low step of 20-30 cm with controlled descent.
Sedentary women train twice a week for 15-20 min at low-moderate intensity.
Active women train three times a week for 20-30 min at moderate intensity with dynamic and reaction exercises.
Athletes train three to four times a week for 25-35 min at controlled moderate-high intensity, without high impact.
Clinical recommendation is two to three sessions per week of 15-30 min, progressing from stable stances to single-leg, unstable surfaces and dynamic movements.

Sample micro-session: 5 min warm-up, 10-15 min main block (single-leg stance 2x20 s, step-down 2x10, lateral shuffle 2x4 m round trip, bird dog 2x10, eyes-closed single-leg 2x20 s), 3-4 min cool-down.
In the third trimester keep difficulty moderate, add support points, lower step height, avoid jumps and lengthen rests.
One concurrent exercise intervention showed improved newborn neuromotor scores at 1 month, though it was not focused only on balance.
takeaways: Progress gradually: bilateral stable stance, single-leg, unstable surface, movement, then eyes closed at advanced level.
Practice next to a chair, bar or wall for support.
Use balance work as a warm-up, a separate block or part of the cool-down.
Keep the space obstacle-free and use safe equipment such as balls, discs and bands.
Begin with an assessment of balance level, history and any lumbopelvic discomfort.
cautions: Avoid sudden position changes, jumps and very unstable surfaces without supervision.
Avoid unstable surfaces if dizziness, loss of control or increased intra-abdominal pressure occur, and avoid prolonged single-leg stance if pelvic pain is present.
Be alert to obstetric warning signs, and avoid prolonged supine positions and abdominal doming.
